title: Naso: confess and repay (Numbers 5:6–7)
hookLine: a wrong is confessed aloud and repaid with a fifth added

lines: YOUR MOUTH, AND A LITTLE EXTRA.
cards: You borrowed your neighbor's ladder in March and it's now October. Or you dinged a friend's car door in a parking lot and drove off, and it's been nagging at you for a year. You could quietly return the ladder.
You could slip some cash in an envelope. It's tempting to fix things in a way that skips saying anything out loud. Today's verses in Naso include two steps that are easy to skip.
One of them is your mouth. The other is your wallet, plus a little.

teach.h: A WRONG TO A NEIGHBOR, A TRESPASS.
teach.b: Numbers five, verses six and seven. When a man or a woman wrongs another person, the Torah calls it a trespass against the LORD. Notice that: cheating your neighbor isn't only between the two of you.
Then the remedy: "then they shall confess their sin which they have done." After that, they repay the full amount, add a fifth on top, and give it to the person they wronged. Two steps, in order.
First, the mouth. Then the money. The verse's verb is vehitvadu, they shall confess, and from it comes the name for this first step: vidui, confession, owning it.
Maimonides builds a whole teaching on this verse.
Real repentance, he writes, includes saying it in words: I did this, I regret it, I'm ashamed of it, I won't do it again. Thinking it isn't enough. The words make it real, to you as much as anyone.
On Yom Kippur, the confessions are said aloud, together, in the plural: we have sinned, we have done wrong.

teach.h: THEN THE MONEY, PLUS A FIFTH.
teach.b: Then the fifth. Returning what you took only puts things back where they were. The added fifth admits the other person lost more than an object: time, trust, sleep, the use of their ladder all summer.

The rabbis worked out the arithmetic: the fifth is counted so that it's a fifth of the total you hand over. And if the wronged person has died with no relatives, the verse says, the payment doesn't vanish.
It goes to the priest. A debt like this doesn't just expire.

how: Jewish tradition sees verbal confession, vidui, as part of repentance; on Yom Kippur the congregation recites the confessions together, aloud and in the plural, and wrongs against people are repaired by making restitution and seeking their forgiveness.

games.why: "then they shall confess their sin which they have done." the mouth comes first; then the full repayment, plus a fifth.

practice: Look for one small wrong you still owe for, the ladder, a forgotten favor, a cutting remark, and picture the person. Find the words, short and plain, I did this, and I'm sorry, and say them silently.
Then think of the fifth, the extra that admits their loss: a coffee with the returned book, a full tank with the borrowed car.

wordCard.voice: Vidui. Confession: owning a wrong out loud, the first step before repaying it, and the root of the Yom Kippur prayers.
